Neonates of Daphnia ambigua emerge from the brood chamber with a body length of only 0.041 cm [Lb = 0.041 cm], a diminutive size that nonetheless equips them for immediate filter-feeding on suspended algae. These newborns are released as fully formed juveniles, bypassing any free-living larval stage, and they begin grazing on phytoplankton within hours of their release. The initial growth trajectory is remarkably steep, driven by high ingestion rates in the nutrient-rich waters of temperate ponds and lakes where this species commonly occurs. Field surveys typically report that the total body length at birth is a consistent trait across populations, though slight variations may arise depending on maternal investment and the quality of available food resources. The small size at birth imposes a vulnerability to invertebrate predators, such as copepods and larval insects, which can capture neonates more readily than larger conspecifics. This selection pressure for rapid growth is a defining feature of the species' life history strategy, as individuals must quickly outgrow the gape-size limitations of many common predators. The measured value of 0.041 cm [Lb = 0.041 cm] for neonatal length aligns closely with published estimates for other members of the genus Daphnia, underscoring a general pattern of relatively small offspring production across this group of cladocerans. This initial investment per offspring is offset by high fecundity over the adult lifespan.

Subsequent growth and life-history timing in Daphnia ambigua have been characterized under a stable rearing temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Individuals reach sexual maturity, or puberty, at a body length of 0.083 cm [Lp = 0.083 cm], attained approximately 14 days after birth [tp = approximately 14 days after birth] at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Growth continues thereafter until animals approach an ultimate body length of 0.136 cm [Li = 0.136 cm], corresponding to an ultimate dry weight of approximately 16.1 micrograms . The maximum lifespan recorded under these same thermal conditions is 147 days [am = 147 days] at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C].
